title: Semantic Web, Ontologies and Knowledge Graphs
oneLiner: Store facts as small subject–relation–object links that machines can follow and reason over, so search and AI can work with meaning instead of just words.

what.html:
A knowledge graph stores facts like "Rahul — ordered — Margherita" and "Margherita — costs — 250". Facts that share a thing link up into a network you can walk. An ontology adds the rules of the domain (a Pizza is a kind of Food; "is inside of" chains along), so a computer can work out facts nobody wrote down.

Everyday versionIf a friend says "my apple cost 80,000", you know it's a phone, not fruit. You used connected knowledge about prices. Knowledge graphs give machines that kind of connected knowledge.

why.html:
• Search by meaning, not just matching words.
  • Answer multi-step questions by following links.
  • Ground AI answers in checkable facts and catch contradictions.

how.title: Words vs meaning
how.html: "cheap laptop repair" shares no words with "Affordable computer hardware fixes", yet it's the best match. Semantic search understands that cheap ≈ affordable and a laptop is a computer.

how.title: Facts as links
how.html: Each fact is subject → relation → object. Shared things join facts into a graph: Rahul → ordered → Margherita → costs → 250 answers "how much did Rahul's order cost?" in two hops.

how.title: Kinds of things
how.html: Say that a Margherita is a Pizza and a Pizza is a kind of Food, and the computer concludes the Margherita is Food, automatically.

how.title: A shared domain model
how.html: An ontology lists the kinds of things (Sandwich, Bread), specific things (this turkey sandwich), and relations (made of, uses bread).

how.title: Rules vs facts
how.html: Keep the rules ("every Student is a Person") apart from the facts ("Rahul is a Student"). Rules plus facts make a knowledge graph.

how.title: Logic on relations
how.html: Mark "is inside of" as chaining (egg in sandwich, sandwich in lunchbox → egg in lunchbox), "pairs with" as two-way, and "has wife"/"has husband" as never both, so contradictions get caught.

how.title: Layer by layer
how.html: IDs for things, then facts, then shared vocabularies, then logic, then huge connected datasets.

how.title: Building one automatically
how.html: Extract facts from text (now often with a language model), map them to the agreed vocabulary, merge duplicates, and check them, because extraction can invent facts.

how.title: Using it
how.html: Graph databases answer pattern questions like "customers whose pizza costs over 300" directly. Knowledge graphs power search info boxes, recommendations and fact-checked AI answers.

demo.html: Ask the pizza graph a few questions and compare a database that treats missing facts as false with a knowledge graph that treats them as unknown.

example.html:
Catching a contradiction. One source says "Ravi has wife Meera", another "Ravi has husband Meera". Each looks fine alone. Because the ontology says those two relations can never both hold for the same pair, a reasoner flags the clash.

Supplementary In these systems, a missing fact means "unknown", not "false": the graph is assumed incomplete.

misunderstandings: It gives structure; vocabularies/ontologies give meaning.
They define classes, properties and logic, not just rows.
takeaways: Semantic search matches meaning; keyword search matches strings.
RDF triples join into graphs; questions are walks.
Ontology (TBox) + data (ABox) = knowledge graph; OWL adds logic.
KGs are built with extraction + validation and used in search, recommendation and Graph RAG.
thirty: Keyword search matches strings ('cheap laptop repair' misses 'affordable computer hardware fixes'); semantic search uses meaning (apple at 80,000 is a phone; author + publisher ⇒ book). RDF states facts as (subject, predicate, object) triples with URIs: Rahul ordered Margherita; Margherita hasPrice 250; isOfType Veg; graphs answer questions by 1- and 2-hop traversal; but predicates need standard vocabularies. RDFS adds rdfs:Class, rdf:type and rdfs:subClassOf, enabling type inference. Ontologies define classes, instances and properties (sandwich ontology). TBox (schema) + ABox (facts) = knowledge graph. OWL adds transitive (egg in sandwich in lunchbox), symmetric (pairsWith), inverse (contains/isIngredientOf) and disjoint (hasWife/hasHusband) properties that a reasoner uses to infer and detect contradictions. The stack: URIs → RDF → RDFS/ontologies → OWL → KGs. KGs are built by extraction (incl. LLMs), entity resolution and validation (DBpedia, Wikidata) and used via graph databases (Cypher), knowledge panels, community detection (Louvain) and Graph RAG.
